text: The bus to school came at 6:40, so I woke at 5:50, and I learned early that mornings are a negotiation I usually lose. I got good at the small wins: the window seat, a song I knew all the way through, the driver’s nod at my stop. Four years of dark winters passed that way, one small win at a time.

My aunt writes letters, real ones with stamps. She tells me about the neighbor’s hip, the price of eggs, and the slow progress of her tomatoes. I answer maybe once in three. Still the envelopes keep arriving, creased and cheerful, as if she needed only to know that someone, somewhere, was holding a pen.

I don’t trust people who say they love all music. Nobody does. We love specific songs: the one from the road trip, the one from the wedding, the one that comes on at the wrong moment and ruins an afternoon. My list is short, embarrassing, and mine, and I defend it the way other people defend their hometowns.

The first time I cooked dinner for my family, I burned the rice, undersalted the chicken, and set off the smoke alarm twice. Nobody complained. My little brother ate three helpings, which I can only call heroism. I have since learned to cook. I have not learned to be as gracious as the people who ate that meal.

Winter in my city is mostly a matter of waiting for the bus, for the thaw, for the plow, for someone to shovel out the corner so you can finally cross. We complain constantly. We also wave at strangers whose cars we have helped push, and that, more than anything on a postcard, is what I mean by home.

There was a boy in my class who never spoke. Not shy, exactly. He seemed to be saving it. In eighth grade he stood to read a poem about his grandmother’s hands, and forty restless thirteen-year-olds went still. I think of him whenever I am tempted to fill a silence with noise.

I have never been good at goodbyes. I linger in doorways, remember one more question, and ask it even when I know the answer. My friends tease me. I would rather be the person who stays too long than the one who walks out without looking at what she is leaving.

My grandmother’s hands were always cold, and she apologized for it every time she held mine. “Cold hands, warm heart,” she would say, and I would roll my eyes. I understand the saying now that there is no one left to say it to. I check my own hands in winter, and they are cold too.

Last spring I joined the debate team knowing nothing. By May I knew how to lose gracefully, which is a skill. We lost almost every round, but we lost loudly and with citations, and our coach bought us pizza after each defeat, as though we had won something only she could see.

I never learned to swim properly. I can stay afloat, mostly, the way a determined cork stays afloat. My friends find this hilarious. I find it useful: it tells me exactly how much I rely on other people, and how little shame there is in holding the side of the pool.
